opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's gotten harder, honestly. The classical Bayesian answer is to put a distribution over the weights and integrate over it, but for networks with billions of parameters that's just not computationally feasible. So people have turned to approximations: variational methods, Monte Carlo dropout, Laplace approximations around the trained solution. In my reading of the empirical comparisons, many of those approximations don't give you very good uncertainty estimates in practice. They tend to be overconfident, especially once you move away from the training distribution.

The approach that has held up surprisingly well is deep ensembles: train several copies of the network from different random initializations and look at how much they disagree. It's not elegant, and it's expensive, because you're training and running five or ten models instead of one. But it's simple and it tends to work. The trouble is that as models get really large, training even one of them is a major investment, so ensembles become impractical. People try cheaper variants, like ensembling only the last layers or using snapshots along a single training run, and those recover some of the benefit.

The direction I find most promising for practical deployment is conformal prediction. It doesn't try to get the model's internal probabilities right. Instead you take a held-out calibration set and use it to wrap the model's outputs in prediction sets or intervals that have a guaranteed coverage rate, say 90%, under the assumption that the test data are exchangeable with the calibration data. It's model-agnostic, so it works with a giant pretrained model you can't retrain, and it's cheap. The catch is that exchangeability assumption. When the world shifts, which in real applications it always does, the guarantee weakens. So you need to pair it with monitoring and with methods for detecting distribution shift and novel inputs.

That gets at a broader point I care about. Uncertainty isn't one thing. There's aleatoric uncertainty, the inherent noise in the problem, and epistemic uncertainty, what the model doesn't know because it hasn't seen enough data. Then there's what I'd call the open-world problem: inputs that belong to categories the model has never encountered at all. Softmax probabilities are notoriously bad at that last case. A network will happily assign 99% confidence to something it has no business classifying. Some of my own work on anomaly detection suggests that what these networks learn is largely a representation of familiarity. They detect the absence of features they know, rather than the presence of something genuinely new.

So my practical advice is layered. Use calibration methods like temperature scaling as a baseline. Use ensembles if you can afford them. Use conformal methods to get guarantees on the outputs. Above all, build in separate out-of-distribution detection and ongoing monitoring, because no single number coming out of a large model is going to tell you reliably when it's out of its depth. And for high-stakes applications, keep a human in the loop who can act on those warnings.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that the picture has gotten both easier and harder at the same time. Easier, because the big models are, in some ways, better calibrated than we expected. If you look at the raw log-probabilities coming out of a large pretrained language model, before any of the fine-tuning and alignment steps, they're actually surprisingly well calibrated on things like multiple-choice questions. The problem is that the subsequent training stages tend to destroy that calibration, because you're pushing the model toward confident, human-pleasing answers. So the information may still be in there, but it's not showing up in the outputs in a trustworthy way.

Harder, because the classic tools we had for uncertainty quantification just don't scale very gracefully. Bayesian neural networks in the full sense were never really practical, and they're certainly not practical at a hundred billion parameters. Deep ensembles were my favorite method for a long time, and they still work extremely well when you can afford them. But training five or ten copies of a frontier model is not a serious option for most people. So we've seen a lot of effort on cheaper approximations: Monte Carlo dropout, last-layer methods, Laplace approximations on just the final layer, and more recently things like LoRA ensembles where you train several small adapters and ensemble those. Those get you some of the benefit at a fraction of the cost, but they tend to capture less of the epistemic uncertainty, which is the part we really care about when the model is operating out of distribution.

I also think it's important to separate the different kinds of uncertainty we're talking about. There's aleatoric uncertainty, the inherent noise in the problem, and models are reasonably good at representing that. There's epistemic uncertainty, where the model simply hasn't seen enough data to know, and that's where we most want it to say "I don't know." And then with these generative models there's a third thing, which is that the output is an open-ended sequence, and asking "what's the probability this answer is correct" doesn't have a clean definition. Semantic entropy, where you sample multiple answers and cluster them by meaning, is one attempt to get at that, and I find it a promising direction, although it's expensive at inference time.

So where does that leave a practitioner? My honest assessment is that for the moment the most practical approaches are the post-hoc ones. Conformal prediction is a big one. It gives you distribution-free coverage guarantees, it treats the model as a black box, and it works with any model of any size. The guarantee is only marginal, and it assumes exchangeability between your calibration data and deployment data, which is exactly the assumption that breaks when the world shifts. But at least it's an honest guarantee with stated assumptions, which is more than most of our methods offer. Alongside that, temperature scaling and other simple recalibration methods on a held-out set remain embarrassingly effective relative to their cost.

The other thing I keep emphasizing is that uncertainty quantification shouldn't be the only line of defense. We also need separate mechanisms for detecting that we're out of distribution at all, because a model can be beautifully calibrated in distribution and still confidently wrong on novel inputs. And ultimately, you want the uncertainty estimates to feed into a system that can actually do something with them, like escalating to a human or declining to answer. A probability that nobody acts on isn't buying you much.

So I'd say we have a toolbox of partial solutions. None of them is fully satisfying for very large models, but the combination of recalibration, conformal methods, cheap partial ensembles, and out-of-distribution detection gets you something usable. The deeper problem, giving a model genuine self-knowledge about the limits of what it knows, I think is still open.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think we have to distinguish two kinds of uncertainty. One is the variability inherent in the problem—there may simply not be enough information in the input to predict the outcome precisely. The other is uncertainty because we haven’t learned enough, or because the example we’re being asked to predict is different from the examples we trained on.

For that second kind, a practical approach is to train an ensemble of networks and look at how much they disagree. It’s relatively straightforward, but as the networks get larger, training several of them becomes expensive. You can use approximations, such as dropout at prediction time or Bayesian treatments of just the final layer, but those give you a more limited picture of uncertainty.

And the important caveat is that agreement doesn’t necessarily mean confidence is justified. All the models may have learned the same wrong thing. So I’d want to evaluate calibration on held-out data and then separately ask what happens when the input distribution changes. Conformal prediction can also be useful for constructing prediction sets, provided its assumptions are appropriate.

So I don’t think there’s a single method that solves this. The practical choice depends on your computational budget, the kinds of changes you expect to encounter, and what action the system can take when it’s uncertain. Can it abstain? Can it ask a person? That’s what makes an uncertainty estimate useful.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think we have to distinguish two sources of uncertainty. One is the variability inherent in the problem—you may simply not have enough information in the input to predict the outcome. The other is uncertainty because the model hasn’t seen enough relevant data. Those call for somewhat different approaches.

The Bayesian approach is very attractive conceptually, because we would like to average over plausible models rather than trust a single fitted model. But with a large deep network, representing and computing that distribution is difficult, and the approximations can matter a great deal.

A practical alternative is to train an ensemble of networks and look at their disagreement. That’s computationally expensive, but fairly straightforward. There are also approaches such as dropout at prediction time that give you a less expensive approximation. The important caveat is that agreement doesn’t establish that the models are right. They can all share the same blind spots.

So I would evaluate uncertainty estimates against the decisions they’re intended to support. When the system says it’s very confident, is it actually correct at the corresponding rate? And what happens when the input distribution changes? Calibration on held-out data is useful, but it doesn’t establish reliability in a new environment. For practical systems, I think uncertainty estimation needs to be coupled with monitoring and the ability to abstain or ask for help.
